lesson.title: When data goes wrong: handling an incident
lesson.subtitle: Contain, report, assess, notify, learn

video.title: When data goes wrong: handling an incident
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds; narration in the lesson language, captions as separate files.
cast: Dr Farah Rahman — university lecturer in education (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

chapters.label: A phone lost on the bus
Assess, notify, and what never helps

scenes.visual: A bus stop. Mr Okafor pats his empty pockets, then opens his bag: no phone.
scenes.animation: The bus pulls away; his hands search his bag.
scenes.narration: My phone was in my bag on the bus this morning. Now it’s gone. It has the class groups, pupils’ phone numbers and photos of their marks. Where do I even start?

scenes.visual: Title card with the Darsi mark and the course name.
scenes.narration: Today: what to do when school data goes wrong, step by step.

scenes.visual: Four incident cards: a lost phone, a message to the wrong group, an email sending scams, a USB stick left in a cyber café.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in as each is named.
scenes.narration: A data incident is any time personal data is lost, stolen or seen by the wrong people. A lost phone. Marks sent to the wrong group. A hacked email sending scams. A USB stick with exam papers, left in a cyber café.

scenes.visual: Five steps joined by arrows: contain, report, assess, notify, learn.
scenes.animation: Each node lights up as it is named.
scenes.narration: When it happens, follow five steps. Contain it, so the damage stops spreading. Report it the same day. Assess what data it was, and whose. Notify the people affected. Then learn, so it doesn’t happen again.

scenes.visual: Four quick actions: a message bin, a phone being locked from a laptop, a new key, an unplugged cable.
scenes.narration: Containing comes first, and fast. Delete a wrong message for everyone, and ask people to delete their copies. Lock or erase a lost phone from another device. Change the passwords. Unplug an infected computer from the network.

scenes.visual: A burst water pipe in a classroom; a teacher turns the tap off, calls the caretaker, checks the wet books, then a plumber fixes the pipe.
scenes.animation: Water stops; a phone call; a wrench turns.
scenes.narration: It’s like a burst pipe in a classroom. First you turn off the water. Then you tell the caretaker, check what got wet, and warn whoever uses the room. Later, you fix the pipe so it doesn’t burst again.

scenes.visual: Dr Farah holds a phone showing a sent message in a parents’ group. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! You’ve just sent the class marks list to the parents’ group by mistake. What do you do first?

scenes.visual: The message disappears with “deleted for everyone”; a teacher walks to the head teacher’s office.
scenes.animation: The message fades; the office door opens.
scenes.narration: Delete it for everyone right away, then tell the head teacher the same day. Ask parents who saw it to delete it too. Telling quickly isn’t a confession: it’s what keeps the damage small.

scenes.visual: The head teacher at a desk with a checklist and a clock.
scenes.animation: Questions tick in; the clock hand moves.
scenes.narration: Next, the school leader assesses. What data was it, and whose? How much harm could it do? If it’s serious, the people affected are told, and often the regulator too. Many laws set a deadline, often seventy-two hours, so report early and let your leader decide.

scenes.visual: Four crossed-out actions: hiding, deleting evidence, paying, arguing.
scenes.animation: A red cross stamps each one.
scenes.narration: A few things never help. Don’t hide it, and don’t delete the evidence: screenshots help. Don’t pay anyone who demands money. And don’t argue with an attacker: report them.

scenes.visual: A phone rings: “IT support”. A speech bubble asks for a code.
scenes.animation: The phone shakes; the bubble pops.
scenes.narration: Many incidents start with a call or a message asking for a code. In the lab, take a call from “IT support”, and choose what to say.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor’s laptop shows his email sending messages to parents on its own. Two answer cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. My email has started sending scam messages to parents. Which step comes first?

scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right.
scenes.on_screen_text: Contain · Report · Assess and notify · Learn
scenes.narration: Contain it first: change the password and sign out everywhere, then warn parents. Remember the five steps, contain, report, assess, notify and learn, and report early, without blame.

scenes.visual: Farah’s classroom. Groups hold incident cards and talk; one pupil walks to the teacher.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: give groups a card each, a lost phone, a photo sent to the wrong group, a hacked game account. Each group decides the first thing to do, and who to tell.

checkpoints.prompt: You’ve just sent the class marks list to the parents’ group by mistake. What do you do first?

options.text: Wait and hope nobody opens it
Delete it for everyone, then tell the head teacher
Leave the group so nobody can ask you about it

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — contain it at once, then report it the same day.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — every minute more people see it. Delete it for everyone, then tell the head teacher.

checkpoints.prompt: Your email has started sending scam messages to parents. Which step comes first?

options.text: Learn: write down what went wrong
Contain: change the password and sign out everywhere

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — stop the scams first. Then warn parents and report it.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — learning comes last. First stop the scams: change the password and sign out of every device.
